claim: Drosophila encodes a single conserved Tomosyn gene with two splice variants.
source: Drosophila encodes a single conserved Tomosyn gene with two splice variants
evidence: The manuscript describes the genomic structure showing mutually exclusive splicing at coding exon 13 to generate Tomosyn13A and Tomosyn13B variants.

claim: The Drosophila Tomosyn homolog is highly conserved with other Tomosyn proteins, displaying high sequence conservation in critical domains including the C-terminal SNARE motif.
source: The Drosophila Tomosyn homolog is highly conserved with other Tomosyn proteins, displaying high sequence conservation in critical domains including the C-terminal SNARE motif.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1 demonstrate conservation across species.

claim: The C-terminal SNARE motif enables the formation of a SNARE complex composed of the Tomosyn C-terminus and the t-SNAREs Syx1A and SNAP-25.
source: This region enables the formation of a SNARE complex composed of the Tomosyn C-terminus and the t-SNAREs Syx1A and SNAP-25 (Fasshauer et al., 1998; Hatsuzawa et al., 2003; Pobbati et al., 2004; Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature and homology modeling shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The Tomosyn SNARE motif forms a phylogenetically distinct group from other v-SNAREs despite their shared affinity for t-SNAREs.
source: BLOSUM62 alignment using the C-terminal tail of the yeast homolog Sro7 as an outgroup indicates the Tomosyn SNARE motif forms a phylogenetically distinct group from other v-SNAREs despite their shared affinity for t-SNAREs (Figure 1A).
evidence: Phylogenetic tree analysis shown in Figure 1A demonstrates distinct clustering.

claim: A conserved ERG sequence within the C-terminal SNARE motif enables zippering of Tomosyn with t-SNAREs in a complex that prevents association with the SV fusion clamp Complexin.
source: A conserved ERG sequence within the C-terminal SNARE motif enables zippering of Tomosyn with t-SNAREs in a complex that prevents association with the SV fusion clamp Complexin, in contrast to SNARE complexes containing Syb2 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Sequence alignment and structural comparison data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: Drosophila tomosyn is alternatively spliced at exon 13 to generate two splice variants, Tomosyn13A and Tomosyn13B, that encode distinct regions of the WD40 repeat scaffold.
source: Similar to other species, Drosophila tomosyn is alternatively spliced at exon 13 to generate two splice variants, Tomosyn13A and Tomosyn13B, that encode distinct regions of the WD40 repeat scaffold.
evidence: Genomic structure shown in Figure 1E demonstrates alternative splicing.

claim: The sequence of exon 13A is highly conserved across insect genomes, while the 13B exon sequence is poorly conserved.
source: The sequence of exon 13A is highly conserved across insect genomes, while the 13B exon sequence is poorly conserved (Figure 1E).
evidence: PhyloP conservation analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Tomosyn13A is likely the more functionally conserved isoform.
source: As such, Tomosyn13A is likely the more functionally conserved isoform.
evidence: Inferred from conservation data showing exon 13A is highly conserved while 13B is poorly conserved.

claim: Iterative homology modeling of Tomosyn13A suggests it forms a double-barrel structure with three disordered loops projecting from the core WD40 scaffold domain.
source: Iterative homology modeling of Tomosyn13A suggests it forms a double-barrel structure with three disordered loops projecting from the core WD40 scaffold domain (Figure 1F), as predicted for mammalian Tomosyn-1 and Tomosyn-2 proteins (Williams et al., 2011).
evidence: Homology modeling shown in Figure 1F and comparison to mammalian proteins.

claim: Exon 13 encodes one of the loops protruding from the WD40 core, indicating alternative splicing regulates secondary features of Tomosyn beyond its SNARE-binding properties.
source: Exon 13 encodes one of the loops protruding from the WD40 core, indicating alternative splicing regulates secondary features of Tomosyn beyond its SNARE-binding properties.
evidence: Inferred from structural modeling and genomic organization.

claim: TomosynNA1 males are homozygous viable and eclose as adults at similar rates to a genetic background control.
source: TomosynNA1 males are homozygous viable and eclose as adults at similar rates to a genetic background control (n≥95 eclosed flies; Chi-square test, p=0.9163).
evidence: Statistical comparison of eclosion rates between mutant and control.

claim: Homozygous adult females eclosed less frequently, suggesting the existence of sex-divergent roles.
source: Homozygous adult females eclosed less frequently, suggesting the existence of sex-divergent roles.
evidence: Observation of reduced female viability compared to males.

claim: Western blots of control and tomosynNA1 brain lysates with Syntaxin1A antisera demonstrated a 2.7-fold increase in SNARE complex levels in the absence of Tomosyn.
source: Western blots of control and tomosynNA1 brain lysates with Syntaxin1A antisera demonstrated a 2.7-fold increase in SNARE complex levels in the absence of Tomosyn (Figure 1G)
evidence: Western blot quantification shown in Figure 1G with statistical analysis.

claim: TomosynNA1 null hemizygous males displayed a 62% increase in the amplitude of evoked excitatory junctional currents (eEJCs) in 0.3 mM extracellular Ca2+.
source: TomosynNA1 null hemizygous males displayed a 62 % increase in the amplitude of evoked excitatory junctional currents (eEJCs) in 0.3 mM extracellular Ca2+, indicating Tomosyn suppresses neurotransmitter release (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A-C with quantification.

claim: A similar 51% increase in evoked release was found in the tomosynFS1 frameshift mutant.
source: A similar 51 % increase in evoked release was found in the tomosynFS1 frameshift mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: Electrophysiological data from independent allele shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Quantal size as measured by miniature excitatory junctional current (mEJC) amplitude was unchanged in tomosynNA1.
source: Quantal size as measured by miniature excitatory junctional current (mEJC) amplitude was unchanged in tomosynNA1 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: mEJC amplitude measurements shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Tomosyn mutant terminals released 70% more SVs across the active zone (AZ) population in response to a single stimulus.
source: Instead, tomosyn mutant terminals released 70 % more SVs across the active zone (AZ) population in response to a single stimulus (Figure 2G and H), with an average increase in quantal content from 84 SVs released in controls to 143 in tomosynNA1.
evidence: Quantal content calculations shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: In higher extracellular Ca2+ (2.0 mM) saline, evoked responses in tomosynNA1 remained larger and displayed a slower evoked charge transfer that resulted in a 43% increase in EJC area.
source: In higher extracellular Ca2+ (2.0 mM) saline, evoked responses in tomosynNA1 remained larger and displayed a slower evoked charge transfer that resulted in a 43 % increase in EJC area (Figure 2I–M).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings in 2.0 mM Ca2+ shown in Figure 2I-M.

claim: The enhancement in delayed SV release is consistent with Drosophila RNAi knockdowns and tomosyn mutants in other species.
source: The enhancement in delayed SV release is consistent with Drosophila RNAi knockdowns and tomosyn mutants in other species (Chen et al., 2011; Gracheva et al., 2006; McEwen et al., 2006; Sakisaka et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparison to published literature on tomosyn function.

claim: TomosynNA1 mutants showed a 3.5-fold increase in the rate of stimulation-independent spontaneous miniature release events.
source: TomosynNA1 mutants also showed a 3.5-fold increase in the rate of stimulation-independent spontaneous miniature release events (Figure 2N and O)
evidence: Mini frequency measurements shown in Figure 2N and O.

claim: The increased mini frequency phenotype was not reported in C. elegans or mammalian Tomosyn-1 mutants though present in mammalian Tomosyn-2 mutants.
source: a phenotype not reported in C. elegans or mammalian Tomosyn-1 mutants though present in mammalian Tomosyn-2 mutants (Geerts et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison to published literature on tomosyn mutants in other species.

claim: Both Drosophila Tomosyn and human Tomosyn-1 transgenes rescued the increased evoked and spontaneous release phenotypes in tomosynNA1.
source: Both homologs rescued the increased evoked and spontaneous release phenotypes in tomosynNA1 (Figure 2P and Q).
evidence: Rescue experiments shown in Figure 2P and Q demonstrating functional complementation.

claim: Human Tomosyn-1 suppressed SV release to below control levels and below rescue with Drosophila Tomosyn.
source: Unexpectedly, rescue with human Tomosyn-1 suppressed SV release to below control levels and below rescue with Drosophila Tomosyn.
evidence: Comparison of rescue effects shown in Figure 2P.

claim: Human Tomosyn-1 was more abundant in presynaptic terminals than Drosophila Tomosyn.
source: Immunohistochemistry against a Myc epitope attached to the transgenic Tomosyn proteins revealed human Tomosyn-1 was more abundant in presynaptic terminals than Drosophila Tomosyn (Figure 2R and S)
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 2R and S.

claim: Dosage-sensitive inhibition of SV fusion is likely to account for the enhanced suppression by human Tomosyn-1.
source: suggesting dosage-sensitive inhibition of SV fusion is likely to account for the enhanced suppression.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between higher protein levels and greater suppression.

claim: Tomosyn suppresses both evoked and spontaneous SV release at Drosophila NMJs.
source: Together, these data indicate Tomosyn suppresses both evoked and spontaneous SV release at Drosophila NMJs, with these properties retained in human Tomosyn-1.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological data from Figures 2 and rescue experiments.

claim: Both Tomosyn13A and 13B splice variants restored neurotransmitter release in tomosynNA1.
source: Both Tomosyn13A and 13B splice variants restored neurotransmitter release in tomosynNA1 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Rescue experiments with different splice variants shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Eliminating the SNARE motif from either splice isoform abolished rescue.
source: Eliminating the SNARE motif from either splice isoform abolished rescue
evidence: Structure-function analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expressing the Tomosyn SNARE domain alone only partially rescued enhanced release.
source: while expressing the Tomosyn SNARE domain alone only partially rescued enhanced release (Figure 3A).
evidence: Rescue experiments with SNARE-only construct shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The SNARE motif is necessary for Tomosyn function.
source: Although the SNARE motif is necessary for Tomosyn function, the failure of the SNARE-only construct to fully rescue release defects suggests the scaffold domain also contributes.
evidence: Inferred from partial rescue by SNARE domain alone.

claim: Co-expression of the scaffold and SNARE domains as independent transgenes failed to reconstitute full-length Tomosyn function.
source: Co-expression of the scaffold and SNARE domains as independent transgenes failed to reconstitute full-length Tomosyn function, indicating these domains must be linked and act cooperatively to decrease SV release (Figure 3A).
evidence: Co-expression experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Full-length Tomosyn was present throughout the periphery of presynaptic boutons as observed for other SV proteins.
source: Full-length Tomosyn was present throughout the periphery of presynaptic boutons as observed for other SV proteins (Figure 3C and D), consistent with the presence of Tomosyn on SVs in C. elegans and mammals (Geerts et al., 2017; McEwen et al., 2006).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry shown in Figure 3C and D, with comparison to published literature.

claim: Both Tomosyn13A and 13B co-localized with the SV protein Synapsin to a greater extent than with the neuronal plasma membrane marker anti-HRP.
source: Both Tomosyn13A and 13B co-localized with the SV protein Synapsin to a greater extent than with the neuronal plasma membrane marker anti-HRP (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Co-localization analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: Tomosyn13A and the 13A scaffold domain alone (Tom13A-∆SNARE) showed similar SV enrichment, suggesting the SNARE motif is dispensable for SV localization.
source: Tomosyn13A and the 13 A scaffold domain alone (Tom13A-∆SNARE) showed similar SV enrichment, suggesting the SNARE motif is dispensable for SV localization.
evidence: Co-localization data comparing full-length and scaffold-only constructs.

claim: The Tomosyn13B scaffold domain (Tom13B-∆SNARE) was slightly less efficient at localizing this isoform to SV rich sites.
source: The Tomosyn13B scaffold domain (Tom13B-∆SNARE) was slightly less efficient at localizing this isoform to SV rich sites.
evidence: Co-localization analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The Tomosyn SNARE motif alone showed reduced co-localization with SVs.
source: In contrast to the scaffold domain, the Tomosyn SNARE motif alone showed reduced co-localization with SVs.
evidence: Co-localization data for SNARE-only construct shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The scaffold domain functions to enhance Tomosyn SV localization.
source: Together, these data indicate the scaffold domain functions to enhance Tomosyn SV localization.
evidence: Summary of localization experiments showing scaffold importance for SV targeting.

claim: Full-length Tomosyn13A suppressed evoked and spontaneous release by 33% and 40%, respectively, when overexpressed in a wildtype background.
source: Full-length Tomosyn13A suppressed evoked and spontaneous release by 33% and 40%, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Tomosyn13B overexpression was less effective at reducing release.
source: Tomosyn13B overexpression was less effective at reducing release, although the 13B scaffold alone modestly decreased mini frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Overexpression data comparing 13A and 13B isoforms.

claim: Overexpression of the remaining Tomosyn truncation mutants, including the SNARE motif alone, failed to inhibit evoked or spontaneous release.
source: Overexpression of the remaining Tomosyn truncation mutants, including the SNARE motif alone, failed to inhibit evoked or spontaneous release.
evidence: Overexpression experiments with truncation mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tomosyn13A acts as a bidirectional modulator of presynaptic output and requires both the scaffold and SNARE domains to fully regulate SV release.
source: These data indicate Tomosyn13A acts as a bidirectional modulator of presynaptic output and requires both the scaffold and SNARE domains to fully regulate SV release.
evidence: Summary of rescue and overexpression experiments demonstrating bidirectional control.

claim: Most of the evoked response in tomosynNA1 was Syt1-dependent, as double mutants had a large reduction in evoked release compared to controls.
source: Most of the evoked response in tomosynNA1 was Syt1-dependent, as double mutants had a large reduction in evoked release compared to controls (Figure 4A).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings from tomosyn;syt1 double mutants shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Tomosyn;syt1 evoked responses were 86% larger than those of syt1 mutants alone.
source: However, tomosyn;syt1 evoked responses were 86 % larger than those of syt1 mutants alone (Figure 4A and B), indicating Tomosyn inhibits release independent of Syt1.
evidence: Quantification of evoked responses in double mutants shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Asynchronous release was increased 1.7-fold in tomosyn;syt1 double mutants compared to syt1 alone.
source: Asynchronous release was increased 1.7-fold in tomosyn;syt1 double mutants compared to syt1 alone (Figure 4C–F), indicating Tomosyn reduces both synchronous and asynchronous SV fusion.
evidence: Analysis of asynchronous release component shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: The elevated mini frequency normally observed in syt1 was enhanced 2.8-fold in tomosyn;syt1 double mutants.
source: Similar to Tomosyn suppression of spontaneous release at wild-type synapses, the elevated mini frequency normally observed in syt1 was enhanced 2.8-fold in tomosyn;syt1 double mutants (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Mini frequency measurements in double mutants shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Syt1 and Tomosyn regulate evoked and spontaneous SV fusion through independent mechanisms.
source: Together, these data indicate Syt1 and Tomosyn regulate evoked and spontaneous SV fusion through independent mechanisms.
evidence: Summary of double mutant analysis showing additive effects.

claim: Both evoked release and mini frequency at syt7M1 mutant NMJs was enhanced by loss of Tomosyn.
source: Both evoked release and mini frequency at syt7M1 mutant NMJs was enhanced by loss of Tomosyn (Figure 4I–L), indicating the proteins act through independent mechanisms to negatively regulate SV fusion.
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings from tomosyn;syt7 double mutants shown in Figure 4I-L.

claim: Increased evoked release in tomosyn;;;syt7 double mutants indicate presynaptic output can still be enhanced beyond that observed in the absence of Tomosyn alone.
source: In addition, increased evoked release in tomosyn;;;syt7 double mutants indicate presynaptic output can still be enhanced beyond that observed in the absence of Tomosyn alone.
evidence: Comparison of evoked release in single and double mutants.

claim: Loss of Tomosyn enhanced release across the entire Ca2+ range but did not alter the Ca2+ cooperativity of release.
source: Loss of Tomosyn enhanced release across the entire Ca2+ range but did not alter the Ca2+ cooperativity of release (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Ca2+ titration experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: At interstimulus intervals (ISI) of 25 and 50 msec, tomosyn mutants displayed enhanced paired-pulse facilitation (PPF).
source: At interstimulus intervals (ISI) of 25 and 50 msec, tomosyn mutants displayed enhanced paired-pulse facilitation (PPF).
evidence: Paired-pulse experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: At 75 ms ISI, PPF is preserved but not significantly enhanced.
source: At 75 ms ISI, PPF is preserved but not significantly enhanced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Paired-pulse data at different ISIs shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, F.

claim: The preservation of PPF suggests Tomosyn is unlikely to reduce fusogenicity of individual SVs.
source: The preservation of PPF suggests Tomosyn is unlikely to reduce fusogenicity of individual SVs.
evidence: Inference from PPF data showing normal facilitation properties.

claim: Tomosyn inhibits SV release through a Ca2+-independent mechanism.
source: Given tomosyn mutants do not decrease the Ca2+ dependence of fusion or PPF, Tomosyn inhibits SV release through a Ca2+-independent mechanism.
evidence: Summary of Ca2+ titration and PPF experiments.

claim: Loss of Tomosyn leads to enhanced synchronous and asynchronous release, together with elevated rates of spontaneous SV fusion.
source: Loss of Tomosyn also leads to enhanced synchronous and asynchronous release, together with elevated rates of spontaneous SV fusion.
evidence: Summary of multiple electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Tomosyn controls SV supply independent of the specific route for SV release, likely by sequestering free t-SNAREs to reduce fusogenic SNARE complex formation.
source: These data indicate Tomosyn controls SV supply independent of the specific route for SV release, likely by sequestering free t-SNAREs to reduce fusogenic SNARE complex formation.
evidence: Inference from multiple lines of evidence including SNARE complex levels and release phenotypes.

claim: AZ number was unchanged at tomosyn synapses.
source: Immunostaining for the AZ scaffold protein Bruchpilot (BRP) demonstrated AZ number was unchanged at tomosyn synapses (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: BRP immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: BRP abundance at individual AZs was not altered.
source: Additionally, BRP abundance at individual AZs was not altered (Figure 5C), indicating release site number and AZ scaffold accumulation are not affected.
evidence: Quantification of BRP intensity per AZ shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Despite a slightly smaller bouton area at Ib NMJs, total NMJ area was unchanged due to a mild increase in the number of boutons per NMJ.
source: Despite a slightly smaller bouton area at Ib NMJs, total NMJ area was unchanged due to a mild increase in the number of boutons per NMJ (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: Morphological analysis shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Is terminals showed no morphological differences from controls.
source: Is terminals showed no morphological differences from controls (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Morphological measurements for Is terminals shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Total SV abundance was not altered in tomosyn mutants.
source: Immunostaining for Syt1 revealed total SV abundance was not altered in tomosyn mutants (Figure 5G–H).
evidence: Syt1 immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Morphological defects or AZ number are unlikely to account for enhanced SV release.
source: Together, these data indicate morphological defects or AZ number are unlikely to account for enhanced SV release.
evidence: Summary of morphological analysis showing no major structural changes.

claim: Ib terminals had a 52% increase in the number of docked SVs per AZ in tomosynNA1.
source: Despite no gross changes to bouton ultrastructure (Figure 6A), Ib terminals had a 52 % increase in the number of docked SVs per AZ in tomosynNA1 (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: TEM analysis and quantification shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Increased docking was observed over the entire length of the AZ, with no change in the absolute fraction of docked SVs along the 400 nm trajectory from the electron dense T-bar center.
source: Increased docking was observed over the entire length of the AZ, with no change in the absolute fraction of docked SVs along the 400 nm trajectory from the electron dense T-bar center (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Spatial distribution analysis of docked SVs shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: The average distance between neighboring SVs was unchanged.
source: The average distance between neighboring SVs was also unchanged (Figure 6F), suggesting SV clustering is not altered.
evidence: SV spacing measurements shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Tomosyn mutants showed a larger number of SVs within 100 and 150 nm concentric circles positioned over the AZ center.
source: Tomosyn mutants also showed a larger number of SVs within 100 and 150 nm concentric circles positioned over the AZ center (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: Quantification of SVs near T-bar shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Average SV diameter and SV density were unchanged.
source: Average SV diameter (Figure 6I) and SV density were unchanged (Figure 6J), indicating Tomosyn does not affect SV formation or total SV number.
evidence: SV diameter and density measurements shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: Tomosyn suppresses release by decreasing SV availability at AZs, with enhanced SV docking occurring in the absence of the protein.
source: Together, these data suggest Tomosyn suppresses release by decreasing SV availability at AZs, with enhanced SV docking occurring in the absence of the protein.
evidence: Summary of TEM analysis showing increased docked SVs in mutants.

claim: Low frequency stimulation (0.33 Hz) resulted in a 4.3-fold increase in the EJC area of the first evoked response in tomosynNA1.
source: Consistent with the enhanced single eEJC phenotype, low frequency stimulation (0.33 Hz) resulted in a 4.3-fold increase in the EJC area of the first evoked response, followed by subsequent depression that stabilized at a 1.4-fold increased quantal content per action potential in tomosynNA1 (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Stimulus train recordings shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: At 10 Hz stimulation, tomosyn mutants displayed more robust synaptic depression, with quantal content quickly dropping below control levels.
source: At 10 Hz stimulation, tomosyn mutants displayed more robust synaptic depression, with quantal content quickly dropping below control levels (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: High-frequency stimulation data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: Control NMJs had lower initial quantal content at 10 Hz and showed a gradual depression in release that was eventually equivalent to synaptic output of tomosynNA1 terminals by the 30th stimulus.
source: Control NMJs had lower initial quantal content at 10 Hz and showed a gradual depression in release that was eventually equivalent to synaptic output of tomosynNA1 terminals by the 30th stimulus (Figure 7C).
evidence: Comparison of depression kinetics shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The size of the immediately releasable SV pool (IRP) showed no difference between tomosynNA1 and controls.
source: The size of the immediately releasable SV pool (IRP), approximated by the cumulative number of quanta released within 30 stimuli, showed no difference between tomosynNA1 and controls (Figure 7D).
evidence: IRP size calculation shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The depression rate was dramatically enhanced in tomosyn.
source: However, the depression rate was dramatically enhanced in tomosyn (Figure 7E), indicating Tomosyn normally restricts release from the IRP.
evidence: Depression index analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The recycling rate in tomosynNA1 mutants was not significantly different from controls.
source: The recycling rate in tomosynNA1 mutants was not significantly different from controls, though the RRP size was increased by 42 % (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: Extended stimulation experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The RRP size was increased by 42% in tomosynNA1 mutants.
source: The recycling rate in tomosynNA1 mutants was not significantly different from controls, though the RRP size was increased by 42 % (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: RRP size calculation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Tomosyn is required to support sustained release by limiting the number of fusogenic SVs.
source: Together these data indicate Tomosyn is required to support sustained release by limiting the number of fusogenic SVs.
evidence: Summary of stimulus train experiments showing rapid depression in mutants.

claim: Immunostaining for Tomosyn13A-Clover revealed a 2.1-fold enrichment of endogenous Tomosyn in Ib terminals relative to Is NMJs.
source: Immunostaining for Tomosyn13A-Clover revealed a 2.1-fold enrichment of endogenous Tomosyn in Ib terminals relative to Is NMJs (Figure 7F and G).
evidence: Endogenously tagged Tomosyn expression analysis shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of Ib synapses in tomosynNA1 mutants showed a 3.8-fold increase in evoked EJC area.
source: Optogenetic stimulation of Ib synapses in tomosynNA1 mutants showed a 3.8-fold increase in evoked EJC area (Figure 7H and I).
evidence: Optogenetic stimulation of Ib neurons shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of tomosynNA1 Is terminals revealed no differences in evoked output.
source: In contrast, optogenetic stimulation of tomosynNA1 Is terminals revealed no differences in evoked output, indicating enhanced release in tomosyn mutants is solely contributed from increased SV fusion at Ib terminals.
evidence: Optogenetic stimulation of Is neurons shown in Figure 7H and I.

claim: Higher expression of Tomosyn in Ib motoneurons results in greater intrinsic release suppression.
source: These data indicate higher expression of Tomosyn in Ib motoneurons results in greater intrinsic release suppression.
evidence: Correlation between differential expression and functional effects.

claim: Is motoneurons showed a 2.4-fold higher average AZ Pr (0.17 ± 0.007) than Ib motoneurons (0.07 ± 0.004) in control animals.
source: Nerve stimulation in control animals indicated Is motoneurons showed a 2.4-fold higher average AZ Pr (0.17 ± 0.007) than Ib motoneurons (0.07 ± 0.004).
evidence: Optical quantal analysis shown in Figure 7J-L.

claim: TomosynFS1 mutants displayed higher Pr at Ib AZs than Is due to increased Ib Pr and no effect on Is Pr.
source: In contrast, tomosynFS1 mutants displayed higher Pr at Ib AZs than Is due to increased Ib Pr and no effect on Is Pr (Figure 7J–L).
evidence: Optical quantal analysis in mutants shown in Figure 7J-L.

claim: Tomosyn suppresses release from tonic synapses and contributes to the intrinsic release differences between these motoneuron subclasses.
source: Together, these data indicate Tomosyn suppresses release from tonic synapses and contributes to the intrinsic release differences between these motoneuron subclasses.
evidence: Summary of optogenetic and optical quantal analysis.

claim: Loss of Tomosyn in Ib neurons changes both the initial Pr and short-term depression properties such that tonic Ib terminals display phasic release similar to Is motoneurons.
source: Loss of Tomosyn in Ib neurons changes both the initial Pr and short-term depression properties such that tonic Ib terminals display phasic release similar to Is motoneurons.
evidence: Summary of functional characterization showing conversion of tonic to phasic properties.

claim: Following addition of Gyki into the extracellular saline, quantal size as measured by mini amplitude was reduced in both control and tomosynNA1 mutants.
source: Following addition of Gyki into the extracellular saline, quantal size as measured by mini amplitude was reduced in both control and tomosynNA1 mutants (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: mEJC measurements before and after Gyki shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Mini frequency was not significantly changed following Gyki application.
source: Mini frequency was not significantly changed following Gyki application, indicating spontaneous fusion events remained detectable (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Mini frequency measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Control animals compensated for the reduction in quantal size with a 62% increase in quantal content that preserved the original evoked response amplitude.
source: Control animals compensated for the reduction in quantal size with a 62 % increase in quantal content that preserved the original evoked response amplitude (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: PHP measurements in controls shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: Tomosyn NMJs showed no significant enhancement in quantal content after Gyki application, indicating PHP expression is impaired.
source: In contrast, tomosyn NMJs showed no significant enhancement in quantal content after Gyki application, indicating PHP expression is impaired.
evidence: PHP measurements in tomosyn mutants shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: In elevated Ca2+, quantal content was greater than after Gyki-induced potentiation in low Ca2+ for controls (46% increase) and tomosynNA1 (61% increase).
source: In elevated Ca2+, quantal content was greater than after Gyki-induced potentiation in low Ca2+ for controls (46 % increase) and tomosynNA1 (61 % increase), indicating lack of potentiation in tomosyn is not due to release saturation (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Comparison of quantal content in different Ca2+ conditions shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tomosyn is required for normal expression of Gyki-induced PHP and represents a key effector for enhancing presynaptic output during this form of plasticity.
source: Together with the observation that tomosyn, syt7 double mutants displayed even higher levels of evoked release than tomosyn mutants alone in low Ca2+ (Figure 4J), these data indicate Tomosyn is required for normal expression of Gyki-induced PHP and represents a key effector for enhancing presynaptic output during this form of plasticity.
evidence: Summary of PHP experiments and comparison to double mutant data.

claim: Control Ib terminals showed a rapid and robust 1.8-fold increase in average AZ Pr 15 min after Gyki incubation.
source: Control Ib terminals showed a rapid and robust 1.8-fold increase in average AZ Pr 15 min after Gyki incubation (Figure 8G–J).
evidence: Optical quantal analysis of PHP at Ib terminals shown in Figure 8G-J.

claim: Enhanced SV release occurred across the majority of the AZ population.
source: Enhanced SV release occurred across the majority of the AZ population.
evidence: Distribution of Pr changes shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Previously silent AZs were recruited during evoked stimulation following Gyki application.
source: In addition, previously silent AZs were recruited during evoked stimulation following Gyki application (Figure 8G).
evidence: Pr maps showing recruitment of silent AZs in Figure 8G.

claim: Is terminals showed no significant change in AZ Pr or recruitment of silent AZs following Gyki application.
source: In contrast to the robust effect at Ib synapses, Is terminals showed no significant change in AZ Pr or recruitment of silent AZs following Gyki application (Figure 8G and K–M), indicating this form of PHP is predominantly expressed from Ib motoneurons.
evidence: Optical quantal analysis of PHP at Is terminals shown in Figure 8G and K-M.

claim: Tomosyn mutants displayed no significant increase in AZ Pr from either Ib or Is terminals following Gyki application.
source: Tomosyn mutants displayed no significant increase in AZ Pr from either Ib or Is terminals following Gyki application (Figure 8G–M).
evidence: Optical quantal analysis in tomosyn mutants shown in Figure 8G-M.

claim: Gyki-induced PHP is Tomosyn-dependent and occurs exclusively at tonic Ib terminals.
source: Together, these data indicate Gyki-induced PHP is Tomosyn-dependent and occurs exclusively at tonic Ib terminals.
evidence: Summary of optical quantal analysis showing Ib-specific PHP.

claim: Loss of Tomosyn generates synaptic responses and a lack of PHP at tonic Ib NMJs that is similar to that observed in phasic Is neurons.
source: Loss of Tomosyn generates synaptic responses and a lack of PHP at tonic Ib NMJs that is similar to that observed in phasic Is neurons, indicating Tomosyn levels represent a key presynaptic mechanism for generating tonic versus phasic presynaptic output.
evidence: Summary of functional characterization comparing Ib and Is properties.

claim: The conserved presynaptic release suppressor Tomosyn functions in setting presynaptic output and plasticity differences for a tonic/phasic pair of motoneurons that co-innervate Drosophila larval muscles.
source: The findings reported here indicate the conserved presynaptic release suppressor Tomosyn functions in setting presynaptic output and plasticity differences for a tonic/phasic pair of motoneurons that co-innervate Drosophila larval muscles.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings.

claim: Synchronous, asynchronous and spontaneous SV release are all elevated in the absence of Tomosyn.
source: CRISPR-generated mutations in Drosophila tomosyn revealed synchronous, asynchronous and spontaneous SV release are all elevated in the absence of the protein.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological characterization of tomosyn mutants.

claim: While single evoked responses were enhanced, rapid depression of release was observed during train stimulation, suggesting loss of Tomosyn biases synapses toward a more phasic pattern of SV release.
source: While single evoked responses were enhanced, rapid depression of release was observed during train stimulation, suggesting loss of Tomosyn biases synapses toward a more phasic pattern of SV release.
evidence: Summary of stimulus train experiments.

claim: Optogenetic experiments revealed a 4-fold increase in output from Ib neurons with no change to Is release.
source: These experiments revealed a 4-fold increase in output from Ib neurons with no change to Is release.
evidence: Summary of optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: Optical quantal analysis confirmed the Ib specific effect of Tomosyn and demonstrated enhanced evoked responses in tomosyn is due to higher intrinsic Pr across the entire AZ population.
source: Optical quantal analysis confirmed the Ib specific effect of Tomosyn and demonstrated enhanced evoked responses in tomosyn is due to higher intrinsic Pr across the entire AZ population.
evidence: Summary of optical quantal analysis results.

claim: Endogenously-tagged Tomosyn was more abundant at Ib synapses than Is, consistent with Tomosyn's role in regulating Ib release.
source: Endogenously-tagged Tomosyn was more abundant at Ib synapses than Is, consistent with Tomosyn's role in regulating Ib release.
evidence: Immunostaining of endogenously tagged Tomosyn showing differential expression.

claim: The intrinsically high Pr and rapid depression normally found in Is motoneurons is due in part to a lack of Tomosyn inhibition of SV usage at phasic synapses.
source: Together, these data indicate the intrinsically high Pr and rapid depression normally found in Is motoneurons is due in part to a lack of Tomosyn inhibition of SV usage at phasic synapses.
evidence: Summary of findings relating Tomosyn expression to release properties.

claim: Tomosyn does not regulate the size of the immediately releasable SV pool (IRP) but rather regulates IRP usage to ensure sustained availability of SVs during prolonged stimulation.
source: High-frequency stimulation experiments demonstrate Tomosyn does not regulate the size of the immediately releasable SV pool (IRP) but rather regulates IRP usage to ensure sustained availability of SVs during prolonged stimulation, as the IRP is strongly biased towards early release in tomosyn mutants.
evidence: Summary of stimulus train analysis showing normal IRP size but altered usage.

claim: Drosophila synapses are more phasic in release character by default, with tonic release requiring higher levels of Tomosyn to generate a fusion bottleneck that enables extended periods of stable release by slowing the rate of SV usage.
source: We propose a model where Drosophila synapses are more phasic in release character by default, with tonic release requiring higher levels of Tomosyn to generate a fusion bottleneck that enables extended periods of stable release by slowing the rate of SV usage.
evidence: Proposed model based on integration of all experimental findings.

claim: The most widely hypothesized mechanism is that Tomosyn competes with Syb2 for binding t-SNAREs.
source: The most widely hypothesized mechanism is that Tomosyn competes with Syb2 for binding t-SNAREs.
evidence: Statement of prevailing hypothesis in the field.

claim: By forming fusion-incompetent SNARE complexes that must be disassembled by NSF, a pool of t-SNAREs is kept in reserve and can be mobilized by alleviating Tomosyn inhibition.
source: By forming fusion-incompetent SNARE complexes that must be disassembled by NSF, a pool of t-SNAREs is kept in reserve and can be mobilized by alleviating Tomosyn inhibition.
evidence: Mechanistic explanation based on known SNARE biology.

claim: Enhanced SNARE complex formation was found in Drosophila tomosyn mutants, consistent with the model that Tomosyn's SNARE domain acts as a decoy SNARE to inhibit productive SNARE complex assembly.
source: Indeed, enhanced SNARE complex formation was found in Drosophila tomosyn mutants, consistent with the model that Tomosyn's SNARE domain acts as a decoy SNARE to inhibit productive SNARE complex assembly.
evidence: Western blot data showing increased SNARE complexes in mutants.

claim: Expression of the Tomosyn scaffold alone failed to rescue the null phenotype.
source: Expression of the Tomosyn scaffold alone failed to rescue the null phenotype
evidence: Rescue experiments with scaffold-only constructs.

claim: Overexpression of the scaffold had no effect on evoked release.
source: while overexpression of the scaffold had no effect on evoked release.
evidence: Overexpression experiments with scaffold constructs.

claim: The scaffold does not directly inhibit fusion.
source: As such, these data indicate that while the scaffold is required for full Tomosyn function, it does not directly inhibit fusion.
evidence: Inference from rescue and overexpression experiments.

claim: Characterization of Drosophila tomosyn/syt1 double mutants demonstrated Tomosyn suppresses release independent of Syt1.
source: Characterization of Drosophila tomosyn/syt1 double mutants demonstrated Tomosyn suppresses release independent of Syt1, arguing the scaffold must serve a function that enhances the inhibitory activity of the SNARE domain independent of Syt1.
evidence: Double mutant analysis showing additive effects.

claim: The Tomosyn SNARE motif was mislocalized without the WD40 scaffold.
source: Indeed, we found the Tomosyn SNARE motif was mislocalized without the WD40 scaffold, arguing this region indirectly supports Tomosyn's inhibitory activity by ensuring proper localization so the SNARE domain can compete for t-SNARE binding.
evidence: Localization experiments with truncation constructs.

claim: Drosophila Tomosyn co-localized with other SV proteins.
source: Similar to studies in C. elegans and mammals, we find Drosophila Tomosyn co-localized with other SV proteins (Geerts et al., 2017; McEwen et al., 2006).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry showing co-localization with Synapsin.

claim: Human Tomosyn transgenes rescued elevated evoked and spontaneous release in tomosyn mutants, indicating functional conservation of its inhibitory properties.
source: Human Tomosyn transgenes also rescued elevated evoked and spontaneous release in tomosyn mutants, indicating functional conservation of its inhibitory properties.
evidence: Cross-species rescue experiments.

claim: Overexpression of either Drosophila or human Tomosyn in a wildtype background also decreased release, demonstrating presynaptic output can be bi-directionally controlled by varying Tomosyn expression levels.
source: Overexpression of either Drosophila or human Tomosyn in a wildtype background also decreased release, demonstrating presynaptic output can be bi-directionally controlled by varying Tomosyn expression levels.
evidence: Overexpression experiments showing dose-dependent effects.

claim: Tomosyn also controls presynaptic homeostatic potentiation (PHP).
source: In addition to intrinsic release differences between tonic and phasic motoneurons, we found Tomosyn also controls presynaptic homeostatic potentiation (PHP).
evidence: Summary of PHP experiments.

claim: Presynaptic homeostatic potentiation occurs when presynaptic motoneurons upregulate Pr and quantal content to compensate for decreased GluR function and smaller quantal size.
source: This form of synaptic plasticity occurs when presynaptic motoneurons upregulate Pr and quantal content to compensate for decreased GluR function and smaller quantal size (Böhme et al., 2019; Frank, 2014; Genç and Davis, 2019; Goel et al., 2019; Gratz et al., 2019).
evidence: Definition of PHP with citations to prior literature.

claim: Inducing PHP with the allosteric GluR inhibitor Gyki revealed Tomosyn is required for expression of this form of acute PHP at Ib terminals.
source: Inducing PHP with the allosteric GluR inhibitor Gyki revealed Tomosyn is required for expression of this form of acute PHP at Ib terminals.
evidence: PHP experiments using Gyki showing lack of potentiation in tomosyn mutants.

claim: Removing Tomosyn inhibition at Ib synapses generates a ~4 fold enhancement in evoked release, more than sufficient to compensate for a twofold reduction in evoked response size from two equally contributing motoneurons.
source: Removing Tomosyn inhibition at Ib synapses generates a ~ 4 fold enhancement in evoked release, more than sufficient to compensate for a twofold reduction in evoked response size from two equally contributing motoneurons.
evidence: Calculation based on optogenetic stimulation results.

claim: AZ Pr mapping revealed Ib synapses potentiate in the presence of Gyki while Is terminals showed no change, indicating enhanced release from Ib is sufficient to homeostatically compensate for Gyki-induced decreases in quantal size.
source: Indeed, AZ Pr mapping revealed Ib synapses potentiate in the presence of Gyki while Is terminals showed no change, indicating enhanced release from Ib is sufficient to homeostatically compensate for Gyki-induced decreases in quantal size.
evidence: Optical quantal analysis showing Ib-specific PHP.

claim: PKA phosphorylation of Tomosyn reduces its SNARE binding properties and decreases its inhibition of SV release.
source: Although future studies will be required to determine the molecular cascade through which Tomosyn mediates PHP expression, prior work indicates PKA phosphorylation of Tomosyn reduces its SNARE binding properties and decreases its inhibition of SV release (Baba et al., 2005; Ben-Simon et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to prior literature on Tomosyn regulation.

claim: Gyki-induced PHP expression requires presynaptic PKD.
source: Given Gyki-induced PHP expression requires presynaptic PKD (Nair et al., 2020)
evidence: Citation to prior work on PHP mechanisms.

claim: An attractive hypothesis is that PKD phosphorylates Tomosyn and reduces its ability to inhibit SNARE complex formation.
source: an attractive hypothesis is that PKD phosphorylates Tomosyn and reduces its ability to inhibit SNARE complex formation.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on integration of current and prior findings.

claim: PKD phosphorylation of Tomosyn could promote SV availability by generating a larger pool of free t-SNAREs to support enhanced docking of SVs at AZs.
source: Similar to tomosyn mutants, this could promote SV availability by generating a larger pool of free t-SNAREs to support enhanced docking of SVs at AZs.
evidence: Proposed mechanism linking Tomosyn regulation to SV docking.

claim: Increased docking would elevate single AZ Pr by increasing the number of fusion-ready SVs upon Ca2+ influx.
source: Increased docking would elevate single AZ Pr by increasing the number of fusion-ready SVs upon Ca2+ influx, similar to the effect we observed with quantal imaging.
evidence: Proposed mechanism consistent with observed Pr changes during PHP.

claim: Despite the importance of Tomosyn in regulating release character between tonic and phasic motoneurons, tomosyn null mutants are viable into adulthood.
source: Despite the importance of Tomosyn in regulating release character between tonic and phasic motoneurons, tomosyn null mutants are viable into adulthood.
evidence: Observation of mutant viability.

claim: The entire range of Tomosyn expression can be used by distinct neuronal populations in vivo to set presynaptic output.
source: As such, the entire range of Tomosyn expression can be used by distinct neuronal populations in vivo to set presynaptic output.
evidence: Inference from viability and differential expression patterns.

claim: Tonic Ib terminals shift towards phasic release with no effect on Is output in tomosyn null mutants, resulting in a collapse of presynaptic release diversity between these two neuronal subgroups.
source: Tonic Ib terminals shift towards phasic release with no effect on Is output in tomosyn null mutants, resulting in a collapse of presynaptic release diversity between these two neuronal subgroups.
evidence: Summary of functional characterization showing convergence of release properties.

claim: Null mutants in syt7 are viable and show dramatically enhanced evoked release.
source: Like tomosyn, null mutants in syt7 are viable and show dramatically enhanced evoked release (Fujii et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to prior work on syt7 mutants.

claim: Tomosyn/syt7 double mutants show even greater increases in release output, arguing multiple non-essential presynaptic proteins can independently fine tune synaptic strength within the presynaptic terminal.
source: Tomosyn/syt7 double mutants show even greater increases in release output, arguing multiple non-essential presynaptic proteins can independently fine tune synaptic strength within the presynaptic terminal.
evidence: Double mutant analysis showing additive effects.

claim: Tomosyn is a highly conserved release inhibitor that varies in expression between distinct neuronal subtypes to regulate intrinsic Pr and plasticity, providing a robust mechanism to generate presynaptic diversity across the nervous system.
source: Together, these experiments demonstrate Tomosyn is a highly conserved release inhibitor that varies in expression between distinct neuronal subtypes to regulate intrinsic Pr and plasticity, providing a robust mechanism to generate presynaptic diversity across the nervous system.
evidence: Summary statement integrating all findings.
